title: Chapter 140 – Ye's Last Name
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Elder Ye]

Ye is a hundred and twenty-four years old, and her left eye has stopped working, and she reads the names in the dark so that she will not have to see how little light she has left.

It is the first week of the eleventh month. The Sutra Hall is closed for the night. The long stacks stand in rows like a forest of paper, dim and enormous, and between them, at the end of the third aisle, a single oil lamp burns on a low table. She sits beside it on a cushion in a quilted gown, with the black stick across her knees and the plum-colored scroll unrolled on the table in front of her. It is nearly all unrolled now. Only a hand's breadth is left curled on the spindle.

Pei Wanli sits across from her with a brush and an ink slab.

He is sixty now, bald and cheerful and stout, with a scar on his left thumb from a net. He was the first. He has not left her side in twenty-four years, except to visit his sister in Lower Weir, and to marry a woman who sells noodles, and to bury his sister, and to marry the noodle woman, and to have two children, whom he calls the Wanlings. He keeps the tally. In a neat clerk's hand, in a ledger bound in blue cloth, he writes down each name as she reads it, and the date, and the one who came to hear.

"Three thousand nine hundred and eighty-seven," he says, and dips the brush.

"I know."

"Thirteen remain."

"I can count."

"Of course you can." He smiles at the page. "I only like to say it. It is a long time, to have been counting."

She grunts. She is not in the mood for being cheerful at. She has a headache behind her good eye, and a pain in her hip that does not go away, and her hands, in the lamplight, on the old brown paper, are the hands of a woman who has been dead for a month and has not yet been informed. But she lifts the scroll to her face and squints, and the characters swim up out of the dark in their tiny upright plum-colored script, patient as ants.

Tuo Ximei. Of the second tannery. Burned in the year 521.

She draws a breath.

"Tuo Ximei," says Ye, in the oldest script. "Who had a harelip, and sang in the choir anyway. Who was born in the year four hundred and ninety-eight, to a woman who tanned hides. Who burned her name at twenty-three to buy her brother a place in the Sutra Hall's school. Who has served the House for forty-one years." She lets the breath go. "Tuo Ximei. You are home."

Nobody answers. Nobody ever answers, in the dark, with the lamp. The name goes out into the stacks and is lost among the rows. Somewhere a thousand li away, she knows, a woman of sixty-four, scrubbing a stone floor in some provincial counting-house, has just straightened up with a cloth in her hand and a strange look on her face. She does not know why. She will weep tonight. Tomorrow she will remember her mother's face.

"Next," says Ye.

* * *

The restored come to the Sutra Hall in a slow river, and she has stopped trying to turn them back.

They arrive in twos and threes, on foot, in the gray dawn: a woman with a bundle, an old man with a cane, a pair of brothers, a clerk in a stained Registry tunic who stands at the gate for an hour before he can make himself knock. They come from the Registry's provincial offices and the Treasury's cellars and the cold stone barracks of the Numbers, and every one of them has the same stunned look, like a man who has woken in a house he does not recognize. They have names. They have not had names in ten years, twenty, thirty. They hold them in their mouths as though afraid of breaking them.

Ye has given them the east wing.

It was a storeroom once, full of moldering scrolls. Now it is a hostel. There are two hundred cots. There is a kitchen, run by Pei Wanli's noodle wife, who has opinions. There is a long table, where they eat, and a long wall, where someone has begun to write the names in chalk. Each person who comes, writes his own. Beside it, if he has them, he adds the names of his parents. By the autumn of the twenty-fourth year the whole eastern wall of the Sutra Hall is a hundred feet of chalk, thick as bark, a field of tiny white characters rising to the ceiling.

She goes to look at it every evening. It is a thing she cannot explain to Wuping, or the Council, or the clerks of the Treasury, who complain of the cost of the grain. It is not a monument. It is not a ledger. It is simply a wall, in a hall, covered with the names of people who are alive, and she stands in front of it with her stick and her one good eye and finds that she is unable to leave.

Tonight there is a girl at the foot of the wall.

She is perhaps nine. She is sitting cross-legged on the floor with a piece of chalk, writing on the lowest row. A woman stands behind her, thin and worn, with her hands clasped tightly in front of her, watching. Ye knows her. She came in the third week of the tenth month. She has said very little.

"What is she writing?" Ye asks.

"My name," says the woman. Her voice is hoarse. "She wishes to put it there herself. She is quite firm."

"How old is she?"

"Nine." A pause. "She was not born when I burned it. She was born after. She grew up in my arms, and I called her little one, and she called me Mother, and neither of us had any other word." The woman's eyes are huge in her face. "I have been Mother for nine years. I was a person for twenty-three before that. I had forgotten that I could be both."

The girl finishes. She stands, wipes her hands on her skirt, and looks up at the wall with her head on one side, studying her work. The character is crooked. It is the best Ye has seen all year.

"There," she says, in a stern small voice. "Now it is true."

* * *

Wuping comes in the second week, with an umbrella and a worried face.

He is seventy, a lean sallow stooped man with a long gray queue and a tendency to apologize before entering a room. He finds her in the stacks, hunched over the scroll in a pool of lamplight, and stands for a moment hesitating at the end of the aisle with the umbrella dripping on the boards. She does not look up.

"Elder Ye."

"Head Wuping."

"I hope I do not intrude."

"You intrude with great delicacy." She turns a page. "Sit. Do not hover. You look like an undertaker."

He sits. He puts the umbrella across his knees. He studies his hands.

"The Council met this morning," he says at last. "About the Second House. About midwinter." He swallows. "They are not all of one mind."

"They never are."

"Treasury wishes to negotiate. Pill Hall would rather not be involved. The Law Elder says the Registry is an unlawful body and that the Court will back her." A faint, helpless smile. "I said that the Court has not been asked."

"What do you say?"

"I say that the Gate is going to fail." He looks up. His eyes are red-rimmed. "I have had two nights without sleep. Lu Fei brought me a reading from the Hall of Weights. The Dock's pulse has dropped by two thirds since the spring. The stair is cold. The Gate wall has begun to... whisper. She says the old men in the east wing hear it at night." His voice cracks. "Ye. You know what it is, better than I. You are taking the Gate's fuel, one name at a time. You have taken it nearly all."

"Yes."

"If the Gate runs dry before the Chain is released..."

"The sleepers will die." She says it plainly. "I know. Jian knows. It has been discussed."

"Then stop."

"No."

"Elder—"

"I am a hundred and twenty-four." She lays down the scroll. For the first time she turns her good eye on him, and in the lamplight it is hard and black and entirely clear. "I have a scroll of four thousand. I have returned three thousand nine hundred and eighty-seven. I have thirteen left. I will finish them. Then I will die. And you, Wuping, will go on being a gentle, frightened man who prefers a quiet life, which is, I may say, no crime." She taps the table. "But you will not ask me to stop at the thirteenth. I have not come this far to hold the last thirteen hostage to the comfort of a Council."

Wuping is silent. Then, slowly, he nods. His shoulders sag.

"No," he says. "I suppose I would not." He lifts the umbrella. "Forgive me. I wished to be able to tell them that I tried."

"Tell them." She picks up the scroll. "Tell them I was very rude."

* * *

Jian comes on the twelfth, alone, in a plain brown cloak, with rain on his shoulders and a look about the eyes that she has learned to read.

He is sixty-two. The years sit on him lightly, as they do on the Purple Mansion, but he has the stillness of a man who carries a full jar and cannot set it down. He finds her in the third aisle and bows, and she tells him to stop doing that, and he sits on the floor beside the table like a pupil. Pei Wanli, tactful, takes the ledger and goes to see about tea.

"Two moons," says Jian. "The Warden gave me two moons. Then the stair, the Dock, the Roll, the Keeper's name, and the dissolution of the Seat."

"You said no."

"I said no."

"Good." She does not look up from the scroll. "Do you know why they ask for the Dock, boy?"

"They think it is the only thing that keeps the Chain from breaking."

"It is. And they are right to be afraid." She turns the spindle a finger's width. "But they have mistaken the cause for the cure. The Chain does not hold the sleepers because the Gate is strong. It holds them because the Gate is fed. When I have read the last name, there is nothing left to feed it. Do you understand what I am telling you?"

He is quiet for a long moment. The rain ticks on the high windows.

"That I am spending the time they have," he says.

"That we are." Now she looks at him, with her one good eye. "I will not pretend it is clean. Thirty sleepers have a clock because I have a scroll. I have thought about it every night for twenty-four years. If you want me to stop, say so now, and I will put it down."

He does not answer at once. She respects that. She has known pupils who would have answered at once, either way.

"No," he says at last. "Finish it. I will wake them another way."

"Can you?"

"I do not know." He smiles, faintly. "But I think I have been wrong before about what I could not do."

She grunts. She reaches out and, to his visible surprise, lays her dry hand on his cheek, the way one does with a child who has fever.

"Go back to your Garden," she says. "Eat something. You look like a candle."

* * *

They come on the night of the thirteenth.

She is expecting it. She has felt it since sundown, in the stiffening of her hip and the thin sour taste at the back of her tongue. The wind has dropped. The lamps in the Hall burn straight up, still as candles in a church. At the third watch Pei Wanli comes into the stacks with his noodle wife's rolling pin in his fist and a look on his face that she has never seen there.

"Elder," he says. "They are at the gate."

"How many?"

"Eighty. Perhaps a hundred." His throat works. "In gray. With the plum seal."

"Is Pei An with them?"

"He is at the front."

She sits for a moment with her hands in her lap. Then she picks up the black stick and uses it to rise, with a grunt, and stands a long time getting her breath, one hand on the table, looking down at the last hand's breadth of paper curled on its spindle. Thirteen names. She knows them all by heart. She has known them since the night Sang Ruo gave her the scroll, in a cold back room, with the autumn light going.

"Help me to the door," she says.

"Elder, it is not safe—"

"I did not ask if it was." She is already moving. "Fetch the white-eyed man, and the four who sleep in the east wing, and the one who stands forty paces behind. And tell my wall to be ready."

"Your wall?"

"Tell them," says Ye, "that the chalk is about to be tested."

* * *

The Sutra Hall's great doors stand open at the top of a flight of nine steps, and at the bottom of the steps, in the light of a hundred lanterns, stands the Second House.

They have not come with swords. That is the first thing she notices. They stand in a loose half-circle on the wet gravel in their gray tunics, a hundred men and women of every age, with their hands folded in their sleeves, and they look, in the cold, like penitents at a funeral. At the front stands Pei An, bearded and tired, with a cloth satchel in one hand. He has aged since the day he sat across a desk from a swordsman and offered him a pill. His eyes in the lamplight are bloodshot.

"Elder Ye," he says. "We have not come to harm anyone."

"That is what the other ones said."

"I know." He bows. "I regret it. I came only for the scroll."

"Why?"

"Because it is eating the Gate." His voice is steady, almost pleading. "You do not understand what you are doing. You think you are freeing them. You are freeing us. You are starving the thing that has held the House together for six hundred years, and when the last name is read, the Gate will go dark, and the Chain will break, and the sleepers will die. Thirty. In their sleep. And we will be left with nothing." His mouth shakes. "I have been a clerk of the House for twenty-two years. I have burned eleven names with my own hand. I did it because I was told it was a kindness. I am an old man, and I find I cannot bear to be told otherwise."

Ye studies him from the top of the steps. The lanterns flicker. Behind her, in the doorway, Pei Wanli is breathing hard, and the white-eyed man has come to stand at her shoulder, and from the shadows beyond the porch come the shuffling steps of the others, the east wing, the restored, the gray silent ones.

"Pei An," she says. "Do you know what the first name on this scroll was?"

He is silent.

"Pei Wanli. A fisherman's son from Lower Weir." She points with the stick. "He is standing behind me with a rolling pin. He has a wife and two children. He was the first." Her voice is not loud. It carries. "I read his name aloud, in an empty room, and he wept for an hour, and then he sang. That is what the Gate has been eating. A man who could sing."

"Elder—"

"You have burned eleven. Eleven. I have all of them. I have yours." She watches his face go slack. "It is on the third inch. Between a weaver and a tanner. You did not know that I knew."

"I—"

"You are not a bad man, Pei An. You are a man who was told it was a kindness." She lifts the scroll in her right hand, and the last curl of paper unrolls on the wind. "I am going to read the last of them now. If you wish to stop me, you will have to come up the steps."

* * *

She reads them one at a time.

It takes eleven minutes. She has never read so slowly, or so clearly. She stands at the top of the steps with the scroll held high in both hands, the black stick tucked under one arm, and her voice, which has been dry and flat for a hundred years, comes out of her like the ring of an old bell. Every name is a stone dropped in a well. She speaks the trade, the village, the debt, the little crooked thing that made each one a person: who kept bees, who was left-handed, who was afraid of horses. She speaks until her breath is gone and her good eye is blind with tears.

The Second House does not move. Pei An's face has gone gray. At the fourth name a woman near the front sinks to her knees. At the seventh, a young clerk drops his satchel and covers his eyes. At the tenth, the entire half-circle is weeping, quite silently, a hundred men and women in gray with the lanterns on their wet faces, and the white-eyed man behind her is making a low steady humming noise in his throat.

Twelve.

She lowers the scroll. Her arms are shaking. There is one name left, a single line of plum-colored script at the very bottom of the paper, small and upright and patient.

She knows it. She has known it for twenty-four years. She read it the first night, alone, in a cold back room, and did not tell Sang Ruo, because it was not a name she wished to say aloud.

The man who stands at her left shoulder, forty paces closer than he has ever been, has lifted his head.

"Yes," says the Nameless. "I know. I have been waiting."

She turns. In the lantern light the face is the same, a face the eye slides off, blank and smooth as a river stone. He is tall and gray. He stands with his hands at his sides. Behind the blankness something is moving, something enormous and old and afraid.

"Do you want it?" she says. "Truly? I cannot take it back."

"I know."

"It will hurt."

"I know." His voice is almost steady. "I have been a ledger for forty-one years. I should like, before I die, to be a man."

She nods. She lifts the scroll. She reads it in the oldest script, slowly, with the whole of her failing breath.

"Ning Ruiyan. Of the eastern port. Who was born in the year four hundred and ninety-five, the third son of a cooper. Who could name every star in the southern sky by his ninth year and was beaten for staring at them. Who burned his name at nineteen to feed his mother through a famine. Who counted the stars in his cell for forty-one years and never once forgot how." Her voice breaks. "Ning Ruiyan. You are home."

* * *

The silence is total.

Then the Nameless makes a sound.

It is not a word. It is not a cry. It is the sound a man makes who has been holding his breath underwater for forty years and has finally been allowed to inhale. His knees buckle. He falls forward onto the steps, onto his hands, and his shoulders heave, and his face, as Ye watches, begins to come back. A broad brow. A short crooked nose. Deep laugh lines. A scar through the left eyebrow. A face she has never seen, lined and plain and utterly human, streaming with tears.

"Ning Ruiyan," he whispers. "Ning. Ning."

He lifts his head. He looks at the lanterns, at the half-circle of weeping clerks, at the old woman above him with her stick and her scroll. His eyes are brown.

"The Southern Fish," he says, in a shaking voice. "The Ladle. The Weaver's Girl. I knew them. I knew them. They were my friends."

Ye smiles. It is the first time she has done so in a decade. She sways, and the white-eyed man catches her, and the scroll slips out of her hand and falls, unrolling, down the nine steps of the Sutra Hall, a long thin banner of plum-colored paper fluttering in the lantern light. At the bottom it comes to rest at Pei An's feet.

It is blank.

Every line. Every name. The ink has gone from it, all at once, like breath from a window. Pei An stares down at the empty paper. Then he drops to his knees, in the gravel, in the lamplight, and begins to laugh and weep at the same time, a terrible helpless sound, and all around him the Second House kneels, one by one, and bows its head.

* * *

They take her to the chair in the third aisle, and she lets them.

It is the one by the lamp, with the quilted cushion. They set her in it gently, the white-eyed man on one side and Pei Wanli on the other, and the Nameless, no, Ning Ruiyan, kneels at her feet with his hands over his face. She has the black stick across her knees. She has the empty scroll in her lap, which someone has fetched. The lamp burns low. Beyond the stacks, in the dark of the Hall, she can hear a hundred people breathing, and the soft chalk-scratch of the east wall as someone, somewhere, begins to write a new name.

She is not afraid. She had expected to be.

"Elder," whispers Pei Wanli. "Elder, please."

"Hush. I am tired."

"Stay a little. Jian is coming. Feng has gone to fetch him."

"Then he will have a long walk." She smiles. "Wanli. Take the ledger. Write it down."

"Write what?"

"That it is done." Her voice is a thread. "Four thousand. Three thousand nine hundred ninety-seven restored. Three who would not hear. Write them all. Do not leave out the three." Her fingers close, weakly, on the stick. "Someone should remember the ones who stayed away."

He writes. His hand shakes.

She looks at the lamp. She has not looked at it properly in years. It is a plain little oil lamp, brass, with a chipped base, the kind they sell in the market for a copper, and its flame is a clean small tongue of gold standing up out of the dark. It reminds her of something. She cannot think what.

A very long stairway, she thinks. And a woman at the bottom, who has already put down the lamp.

"Teacher," she says.

Her voice is a child's. She is nineteen, in a gray tunic, in the winter of the year four hundred and forty-one, in a cold anteroom, and a clerk is handing her a black stick. The Master left this for you. She has worn a groove in the grain. She has oiled it every spring.

She looks up, and at the end of the aisle, at the top of a long dark stair, a small figure stands with a lantern in her hand, and lifts it, and smiles.

"I did not have you for thirty years in order to be remembered," says Sang Ruo. "I had you in order that someone should know how to read."

"I know," says Ye. "I read them all."

The light is very bright. She says one word, the hooked one, the fourth in the Founders' first sentence, and she says it clearly, like a lesson well learned, and the lamp on the table gutters and goes out.

Remain.
